props.title: City of the Living Dead
props.initialSlug: A priest's suicide unleashes zombie horror on Earth

sections.content: Lucio Fulci's City of the Living Dead marks a pivotal moment in Italian horror, launching his unofficial "Gates of Hell" trilogy with surreal nightmare logic and groundbreaking gore effects. Following Zombi 2 (1979), Fulci abandoned traditional narrative coherence for a dreamlike descent into supernatural terror. The film's infamous drill-through-the-head scene and brain-squeezing moments pushed practical effects boundaries, influencing later extreme horror like Hellraiser (1987) and Re-Animator (1985).

sections.content: The film's influence on supernatural horror extends beyond its shocking gore. Its emphasis on atmosphere and religious dread influenced later works like Prince of Darkness (1987) and Event Horizon (1997). The blend of Catholic imagery with Lovecraftian cosmic horror created a template for films like Demons (1985) and Cemetery Man (1994), while its dream-logic approach to narrative prefigured Jacob's Ladder (1990).

Fulci's technical innovations deserve special attention. Cinematographer Sergio Salvati's use of extreme close-ups and fog-drenched exteriors created a distinct visual style that influenced Italian horror for decades. The film's sound design, particularly its use of Fabio Frizzi's synth score, established a sonic template that would influence everything from Suspiria (1977) to modern throwback films like Mandy (2018). sections.content: City of the Living Dead represents a crucial transition point between the giallo-influenced Italian horror of the 1970s and the more extreme splatter films of the 1980s. Its success paved the way for increasingly boundary-pushing works like Demons (1985), Stage Fright (1987), and Opera (1987). The film's practical effects team, led by Gino De Rossi, revolutionized gore techniques that would influence American splatter films like Day of the Dead (1985).
